rationale: A wins because it keeps its shoes on the floor. A's "Can a 1.8B model really match one 4x its size? Hugging Face's own numbers say maybe" turns the benchmark into a testable question; B's "A Fortune 100 manufacturer is running Hugging Face models behind its own firewall" asserts a deployment the update never gave you. B has the sharper business-model headline in "gives away its newest model and starts charging $50 a seat," but then spends that advantage by printing speculative security and firewall angles as if proof already exists.
gaps_in_A: A misses the strongest compression of the business story: it separates "open-sourced model" and "starts charging" instead of making the same-day free-model/paid-control-plane tension the lead.

The next step says "journalist-fit-check" even though the benchmark angle depends on unreproduced company numbers. That claim needs fact-checking or reproducible eval materials before journalist matching.
The customer angle is correctly cautious, but "A Fortune 100 manufacturer is an early customer" remains weak until the actual name and on-record access exist.
gaps_in_B: "A Fortune 100 manufacturer is running Hugging Face models behind its own firewall" invents the firewall and the deployment. The update only says a named Fortune 100 manufacturer is an early enterprise customer.
"lets AI near the plant" decorates the customer story with manufacturing-site drama the facts do not support.
"Two million models, and no easy way to know which ones are safe to use" invents a safety/provenance problem from a bare model-count stat and audit-log feature.
"a commercial admission that pulling arbitrary weights is a governance problem" is clever, but it is inference wearing a fact costume. You need buyer evidence before pitching that.
